description_full: Cresud Sociedad Anónima, Comercial, Inmobiliaria, Financiera y Agropecuaria, an agricultural company, engages in the production of agricultural commodities in Brazil and other Latin American countries. It operates through Agricultural Business, and Urban Properties and Investments segments. The company is also involved in the management, development, and ownership of shopping malls, office buildings, and hotels; sale of grain derivatives, such as flour and oil; production and sale of crops, such as soybean, sugarcane, wheat, corn, oilseed, and sunflower, as well as sorghum and peanuts; and breeding, purchasing, and/or fattening of cattle for sale to slaughterhouses and supermarkets. In addition, it leases its farms to third parties for agriculture, cattle breeding, and seed production; and offers agricultural services. The company was incorporated in 1936 and is headquartered in Buenos Aires, Argentina.
ceo_bio: Mr. Alejandro  Gustavo Elsztain | Second Vice Chairman, CEO, & GM | Age 59
financial_summary: Cresud S.A.C.I.F. y A. is a small-cap industrials business with a $552M market cap on $690M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at -1% over the past three years — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding. Operating margins are contracting by -6.4pp, the first warning that competitive pressure is eroding the franchise.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, with gross margins sitting at 40%.

The business throws off $80M in free cash flow — roughly 12 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.67×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.3× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 3.6×.

Management returns a meaningful 11.9% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 18% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 2.9× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 32% operating margin runs 23pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.91x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-26.6% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 45% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 43% and a beta of 0.89, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 1.11 vs 5y 0.78), so read it loosely.
About $2.4M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 65% in the 2020 crash, 56% in the 2022 bear market and 76% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 61% below its blended-model fair value of $19.95, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 30%), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/E 5.0 vs 22.1 and P/FCF 6.9 vs 21.8 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 45% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 14.4% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 0.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 2 covering analysts target $15.16 on average, 95% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 6% falls short of the cost of capital of 7.6%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.09).
It runs a 40% gross margin and converts 12% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is a concern: cash conversion of only 0.67x.
ROE of 23% is amplified by 5.2x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
Operating margin is running 6pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.3x net debt to EBITDA ($194.2M of cash against $1.0B of debt), with interest covered 3.6x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 0.57 in the distress zone.
The value-trap profile is elevated (50/100); see the breakdown below.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -0.9% over 3 years and -15.6% over 5 years, so the decline is easing, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 46%).
At current returns, reinvesting 62% of profits supports about 3.7% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -26.9% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Analysts expect 29.2% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own 18.0%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 24%.
Insider trading is two-way: 15 purchases and 10 sales over the past year, net $1.5M bought.
It returns 11.9% a year to shareholders (9.6% in dividends).
